compute.note: CONFLICT, parameters left null: VarBench's Hubbard/supplements/Imada_group_overview.md says the RBM has a 4x4 sublattice ("with 4x4 subblattice"), while sub_rbm_phidx.py generates a translation-invariant (1x1) RBM. The script's own architecture would have 66564 complex parameters (formula below), recorded here only. samples = NVMCSample x MPI processes / NSplitSize = 100 x 8 / 1 = 800 per SR step: with NSplitSize = 1 every rank is its own sampling group (vmcmain.c "group1 = rank0/NSplitSize"), draws NVMCSample samples after NVMCWarmUp = 100 (each separated by NVMCInterval x Nsite = 256 proposals) and WeightAverageWE sums the weights over all ranks (average.c); iterations = NSROptItrStep = 1000 SR steps (the parameters are averaged over the last NSROptItrSmp = 100). All of these are the defaults of make_modpara, not overridden by the optimisation call. Each amplitude sums a Pfaffian of the 256-electron pair-product state over NSPGaussLeg x |NMPTrans| = 8 x 256 = 2048 spin/momentum projection points. Doubt (why confidence is low): the script is the simplified template of programs/mVMC_makedef/README.txt ("For simplicity, we focus on the case of Ns=8x8"). It runs ONE optimisation stage with the projections and the RBM on from the start, while the README's protocol has three optimisation stages (f_ij alone from the UHF solution, then the RBM, then the projections) whose step counts are not stated anywhere, and it never runs the Lanczos step the energy includes: make_all.py also writes namelist_aft.def/modpara_aft.def (NVMCCalMode=1, NLanczosMode=1, NVMCWarmUp=500, NVMCInterval=5, NVMCSample=5000, NDataQtySmp=10) but mVMC.sh does not call it. So the counts are the script's single stage, not the published run's total. No time is recorded anywhere; "mpiexec -np 8" names MPI processes, not hardware.

compute.reported_as: We typically choose tau = 0.01 in this work, with which we have verified that the Trotter error is below the targeted statistical errors. || In this section, we present results at half-filling. As mentioned, the AFQMC results are numerically exact, as the sign problem is absent because of the particle-hole symmetry. We use a combination of the path-integral approach [40] and the random walk approach [25]. || In this work, we use a special form of the generalized Hartree-Fock (GHF) [34] wave function as TWF in the AFQMC calculations. This will increase the computation time by a factor of 2 to 4 in different portions of algorithm, because now the Slater determinant of up and down spin are coupled. || Earlier calculations were carried out at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Most of the calculations were carried out at the Extreme Science and Engineering Discovery Environment (XSEDE), which is supported by National Science Foundation Grant No. ACI-1053575, and the computational facilities at the College of William and Mary.
